C.sweetness: Dry to sweet; check the bottle

L.sweetness: Dry to off-dry; check the bottle

J.sweetness: Usually dry; ripe fruit is not sugar

O.sweetness: Dry in the traditional dry style

foods.title: Shellfish

foods.title: Fish

foods.title: Pork & charcuterie
foods.examples: Roast pork, cured meats or a savory pork dish

foods.title: Beef & lamb

foods.examples: Chili heat, aromatic curries or spicy noodles

foods.title: Vegetables & mushrooms
foods.examples: Grilled vegetables, mushroom dishes or vegetarian mains

foods.title: Salads & herbs

foods.title: Creamy dishes
foods.examples: Cream sauces, buttery preparations or rich risotto

A.shellfish: Bright acidity and restrained fruit can complement briny shellfish. Choose a fresh, dry bottle.
A.fish: Fresh acidity works with lemon-dressed or simply grilled fish without overwhelming delicate flavors.
A.salads: A crisp dry style can meet the acidity of a citrus or vinaigrette dressing.
A.vegetables: Citrus and herbal notes can echo fresh herbs and lighter vegetable dishes.

B.poultry: A rounded white with freshness can match roast poultry without dominating it.
B.fish: Pear and citrus notes suit roasted fish; choose a fresher bottle for a lighter preparation.
B.cream: Some texture matches a creamy sauce, while a fresh finish keeps the pairing lively.
B.vegetables: A medium-bodied white can meet roasted vegetables and gently savory flavors.

C.spicy: Choose an off-dry, lower-alcohol bottle: a little sweetness can soften the impression of chili heat. A dry version behaves differently.
C.poultry: A dry style suits roast poultry; an off-dry aromatic style can suit a gently spiced sauce.
C.salads: Choose a dry, high-acid example to complement fresh herbs and an acidic dressing.

D.cream: A fuller white can match a buttery or creamy texture. Oak and butter notes work best when they echo the preparation.
D.poultry: Riper fruit and a fuller texture can stand alongside roast chicken or a richer poultry sauce.
D.fish: Choose butter-roasted or richer fish for a fuller white; lean raw seafood usually calls for a lighter style.

L.spicy: Choose an off-dry bottle with modest alcohol for aromatic spice. Dry, high-alcohol examples may intensify heat.
L.cheese: Perfumed fruit and a broad texture can complement stronger or washed-rind cheeses. Check the bottle’s sweetness.
L.vegetables: Floral and spice notes can echo aromatic vegetable dishes rather than a sharp vinaigrette.

E.poultry: Lighter body and gentler tannins let poultry remain the focus.
E.pork: Freshness can balance roast pork’s richness without a very heavy tannic finish.
E.fish: Choose richer salmon or tuna preparations: gentle tannins are a better starting point than a powerful tannic red.
E.vegetables: Fresh red fruit and earthy notes can complement mushrooms or lightly roasted vegetables.

F.pork: Savory pork and charcuterie can meet medium-bodied red fruit and moderate tannins.
F.tomato: Choose a fresher example so its acidity can keep pace with tomato sauce.
F.vegetables: Roasted vegetables and mushrooms can match a red’s savory fruit and medium body.
F.cheese: Aged or firm cheeses can meet moderate tannins and a fuller fruit profile.

G.beef: Rich meat, fat and protein can soften the impression of firm tannins and match a full body.
G.cheese: Firm, aged cheeses can meet a structured red more comfortably than very delicate fresh cheese.
G.vegetables: Choose a substantial mushroom or roasted vegetable dish to match the wine’s body and savory flavors.

H.tomato: High acidity is a useful match for a tomato-based sauce; the food should have enough substance for the tannins.
H.beef: Rich meat and fat can balance firm tannins, while acidity refreshes the palate.
H.vegetables: Earthy mushroom dishes can echo savory aromas; use a substantial preparation for stronger tannins.

J.barbecue: Ripe fruit can complement smoky char and a mildly sweet sauce. Strong chili heat may clash with high alcohol.
J.beef: A generous body and dark fruit can meet grilled beef or lamb.
J.pork: Ripe fruit and spice notes can complement smoky or roasted pork preparations.

R.fish: A fresh, lower-tannin rosé can bridge light seafood and richer grilled fish.
R.poultry: Red-fruit freshness can complement roast poultry without a heavy tannic finish.
R.vegetables: Fresh fruit and acidity suit Mediterranean vegetables and herb-led dishes.
R.salads: Choose a dry, fresh style for citrus, herbs and a light vinaigrette.

K.fried: Acidity and bubbles refresh the palate after a fatty, crispy bite.
K.shellfish: Choose a dry sparkling style to complement delicate, saline shellfish.
K.cheese: A fresh sparkling wine can contrast creamy cheese with acidity and bubbles.

S.dessert: Choose a wine at least as sweet as the dessert; floral or stone-fruit notes can echo fruit and honeyed flavors.
S.cheese: Sweetness can create a contrast with salty or stronger cheese. Match the wine’s intensity to the cheese.

T.chocolate: Sweetness and dark-fruit flavor can complement cocoa-rich desserts. The wine should be at least as sweet as the food.
T.cheese: A sweet, full-bodied style creates contrast with salty blue or strong cheese.
T.dessert: A rich sweet style can match dried fruit or a substantial pastry. Compare the sweetness levels.

P.dessert: Nutty, dried-fruit or caramel notes can echo nut pastries and caramelized desserts; match sweetness.
P.chocolate: Choose a sufficiently sweet style for cocoa-rich desserts, especially when the wine shows dried fruit or caramel.
P.cheese: Sweetness and concentrated flavor can balance salty or stronger cheeses.

Q.shellfish: Dry, saline and savory notes can work alongside shellfish and salty seafood preparations.
Q.cheese: Dry savory flavors can complement salty hard cheese and almonds.
Q.vegetables: A savory dry style can complement olives, nuts and a vegetable-led tapas plate.

O.cheese: Oxidative nutty notes and a dry finish can complement mature hard cheese.
O.vegetables: Nutty, savory aromas can echo mushrooms and roasted vegetables.
O.pork: A dry, savory style can complement cured meats or a rich pork preparation.

families.title: Old Fashioned-style
families.method: Usually stir with ice; finish with an aromatic garnish.
families.variation: Change the base spirit or sweetener while preserving its role. Sazerac and Japanese Cocktail are related patterns, with their own named specifications.

families.title: Martini & vermouth-led
families.structure: Base spirit + vermouth or aromatized wine
families.method: Usually stir and serve up; Vesper is a documented shaken exception.
families.variation: Change the spirit or wine ratio intentionally. A Gibson uses an onion garnish; El Presidente is a rum-and-vermouth relative.

families.title: Manhattan-style
families.structure: Spirit + sweet wine or amaro + bitters
families.method: Stir, then serve up or in the specified rocks presentation.
families.variation: Black Manhattan replaces vermouth with Averna. Vieux Carré combines rye, cognac, vermouth and an additional liqueur.

families.title: Negroni-style
families.structure: Base spirit + bitter aperitif + aromatized wine
families.method: Stir and use the specified chilled or rocks presentation.
families.variation: A Boulevardier changes gin to whiskey; White Negroni changes the bitter and wine components. Ratios are recipe-specific.

families.title: Classic sours
families.method: Usually shake; egg-white foam is a separate optional choice in specified recipes.
families.variation: Compare the original measured recipe before changing citrus, sweetener or base spirit. A fruit or wine addition changes the individual recipe.

families.title: Daiquiri variations
families.method: Shake classic versions; blend a specified frozen version.
families.variation: Hemingway adds grapefruit and maraschino; Royal Bermuda Yacht Club uses falernum and curaçao. These are distinct measured variations.

families.title: Margarita variations
families.method: Shake; prepare the chosen rim and presentation before pouring.
families.variation: Orange liqueur supplies sweetness in a classic serving. Tommy’s uses agave; mezcal or split bases change the character.

families.title: Sidecar & brandy sours
families.structure: Brandy + citrus + liqueur or sweet component
families.taste: Bright citrus with a rich brandy base.
families.method: Shake and strain into the specified prepared glass.
families.variation: Between the Sheets adds rum; Brandy Crusta includes extra aromatics and a characteristic citrus-peel serving.

families.title: Herbal & liqueur sours
families.taste: Citrus balanced with herbal, floral or bitter flavor.
families.method: Shake and strain; measure the liqueurs carefully.
families.variation: Last Word and Paper Plane use equal-part recipes. Aviation uses different ratios and is not an equal-parts drink.

families.title: Collins & fizz-style
families.method: Shake the non-carbonated mixture, then add bubbles gently.
families.variation: Collins serves over ice; a Gin Fizz commonly uses no serving ice. French 75 adds Champagne rather than soda.

families.title: Highballs & built long drinks
families.method: Usually build over ice; some recipes shake non-carbonated ingredients first.
families.variation: Mules use ginger beer; Rickey uses unsweetened soda; Bloody Mary is a savory, non-carbonated long drink. These are a teaching group, not one fixed formula.

families.title: Mint, juleps & swizzles
families.structure: Base + mint + sweetener; citrus where specified
families.taste: Fresh mint aroma and cold, refreshing texture.
families.method: Press mint gently; churn or swizzle with the specified ice.
families.variation: Julep has no sour structure; Mojito includes lime and soda; Queen’s Park Swizzle finishes with aromatic bitters.

families.title: Tropical & tiki patterns
families.structure: Rum with recipe-specific citrus, fruit or sweet modifiers
families.taste: Fruit-led, complex or creamy depending on the recipe.
families.method: Follow the individual shake or blend method and ice presentation.
families.variation: This is a broad teaching group. Classic Mai Tai has no pineapple; Jungle Bird adds Campari, while Colada and Painkiller use cream of coconut.

families.title: Coffee, cream & after-dinner
families.structure: Base + coffee, cream, cacao or mint modifier
families.taste: Coffee-rich, creamy or aromatic depending on the drink.
families.method: Follow the specific shake, stir or built method.
families.variation: Black Russian contains no cream; White Russian does. Espresso Martini is a shaken coffee cocktail, and Stinger is cognac with white mint liqueur.

families.title: Modern fruit & muddled variations
families.structure: A base with recipe-specific fruit and sweet components
families.method: Follow the named recipe; strain shaken drinks and retain fruit in a Caipiroska.
families.variation: French Martini and Pornstar Martini are named modern drinks without vermouth. Caipiroska is a vodka-and-muddled-lime variation. This is a comparison group.

spirits.name: Whiskey
spirits.taste: Grain, oak and warming spice; fruit, smoke and sweetness vary with grain, origin, aging and cask.
styles: Bourbon
Corn-led whiskey, often with vanilla, caramel and oak; commonly rounded and rich.
Rye whiskey
Often peppery or herbal with grain and oak notes; sweetness and intensity vary.
Scotch whisky
Ranges from delicate malt and fruit to rich sherry-cask flavors or pronounced peat smoke.
Irish whiskey
Often approachable grain and fruit flavors; pot-still, malt and grain styles differ.
Japanese whisky
Styles vary from delicate fruit and oak to fuller or smoky expressions.

spirits.name: Gin
spirits.taste: Juniper-led with citrus, herbs and spice according to the botanical recipe.
styles: London Dry
Typically dry, juniper-led and crisp; citrus and spice vary by producer.
Old Tom
Often rounder or slightly sweetened, with a softer impression.
Contemporary gin
Juniper remains part of gin, while other floral, citrus or herbal botanicals may stand out.
Navy strength
A higher-strength bottling; botanical intensity and dilution need attention.
Genever
A related Dutch/Belgian spirit, often showing maltier flavors; it is not interchangeable with every gin.

spirits.name: Rum
spirits.taste: Sugarcane-derived flavors ranging from light and fresh to rich molasses, tropical fruit, oak and spice.
styles: White rum
Often light and fresh; some white rums are aged then filtered.
Aged rum
Can gain oak, vanilla, dried fruit and spice from maturation.
Dark rum
Color may reflect aging or added color; check the specific bottle’s sweetness and style.
Rhum agricole
Cane-juice rum can show grassy, herbal and earthy flavors.
Overproof rum
Higher strength; flavor and serving measures are recipe-specific.

spirits.name: Tequila & mezcal
spirits.taste: Agave, citrus, herbs and earth; aging and production influence oak, sweetness and smoke.
styles: Blanco tequila
Usually fresh agave, citrus and herbal or peppery notes.
Reposado tequila
Aging can add gentle oak, vanilla and a rounder texture.
Añejo tequila
Longer aging often brings more oak, spice and a fuller impression.
Mezcal
Agave variety and production create diverse herbal, earthy, fruity or smoky styles.
Split agave base
A recipe can combine tequila and mezcal to balance fresh agave and the chosen mezcal’s character.

spirits.name: Vodka
spirits.taste: Often restrained in aroma, with texture and subtle grain, mineral or other base-related differences.
styles: Unflavored vodka
A relatively neutral base that lets mixers and modifiers stand out.
Citrus vodka
Adds lemon or other citrus character; sweetness varies.
Vanilla vodka
Adds vanilla aroma for specified dessert or fruit cocktails.
Other flavored vodka
Fruit, spice and sweetness vary; read the bottle before replacing a neutral base.

spirits.name: Brandy
spirits.taste: Distilled fruit with possible oak, dried-fruit, spice and floral notes; the fruit source and aging matter.
styles: Cognac
Grape brandy from the Cognac region, often with fruit, oak and spice shaped by aging.
Armagnac
Grape brandy from Gascony, often with robust fruit, spice and aging-related savory notes.
Pisco
A grape spirit with fruit or floral aromas; country and grape style matter.
Calvados
Apple or apple-and-pear brandy, with orchard fruit and possible oak notes.
Other fruit brandies
Cherry, plum, pear and other fruit spirits have distinct aromas and may be unaged.

shellfish: A dry, savory gin-and-vermouth serving can suit briny shellfish; keep the garnish and seasoning gentle.
Unsweetened lime and soda provide a light, fresh contrast to gently dressed seafood.
Citrus and bubbles can refresh the palate alongside a richer seafood bite.
fish: A light lime-and-soda structure leaves room for delicate fish.
Lemon freshness can echo a citrus-dressed or grilled preparation.
Lime and agave can complement grilled fish tacos; match rim salt to the dish.
poultry: Fresh lemon and bubbles can balance roast poultry’s richness.
A well-balanced citrus sour can complement grilled or gently seasoned chicken.
A fuller whiskey sour can suit roasted poultry with a savory or lightly sweet glaze.
pork: Oak, bitters and restrained sweetness can echo roast or smoked pork.
A bitter, whiskey-led serving can create contrast with a rich savory bite.
Grapefruit and bubbles can refresh the palate after a fatty pork taco.
beef: A spirit-forward whiskey drink can match grilled meat and char.
Whiskey and sweet vermouth can echo a rich, savory beef preparation.
A bitter, structured serving can contrast with fatty grilled food; personal preference matters.
spicy: Use a balanced, lightly sweet serving for aromatic spice; alcohol can still intensify strong heat.
Sweetness and a creamy texture can contrast with chili; the alcohol strength still matters.
Fruit and a long serving can suit gently spicy tacos; it is not a guarantee against strong chili heat.
vegetables: Herbal bitterness can complement grilled vegetables and a substantial savory dish.
Mint and citrus can echo herbs in a lighter vegetable preparation.
Savory tomato and seasoning can connect with roasted or vegetable-led food.
salads: A light, unsweetened citrus serving can meet a lemon dressing without a heavy finish.
Mint and citrus can echo fresh herbs.
Lemon freshness can complement a citrus-based dressing; balance sweetness thoughtfully.
cream: Citrus acidity and bubbles can refresh the palate after a creamy bite.
Bitterness can contrast with a rich savory sauce; avoid overwhelming a delicate dish.
A lighter citrus highball provides contrast without adding more cream.
cheese: Rich whiskey and vermouth can match mature hard cheese.
Freshness and bubbles can contrast with soft, creamy cheese.
A spirit-led serving can suit stronger aged cheeses and nuts.
tomato: Herbal bitterness can suit a substantial tomato-and-herb dish.
A fuller bitter cocktail can match rich pizza or a meat-based tomato sauce.
A fresh, lighter option can suit a simpler tomato preparation.
barbecue: Oak and measured sweetness can echo smoke and a mild glaze.
Lemon freshness can balance grilled richness and a gently sweet sauce.
A long grapefruit serving can refresh the palate between smoky bites.
fried: Bubbles and citrus provide a fresh contrast to a crispy, fatty bite.
Lemon and soda can refresh the palate after fried food.
Grapefruit freshness can complement lightly seasoned fried food.
dessert: Cream and cacao can complement a rich, moderately sweet pastry.
Coffee flavor can echo chocolate or coffee-accented pastries; sweetness varies by recipe.
Passion fruit can complement a fruit dessert; compare the dish’s sweetness with the drink.
chocolate: Coffee can echo chocolate’s roasted flavors; choose a dessert that does not overwhelm the drink’s sweetness.
Cacao and cream can complement a creamy chocolate dessert.
Coffee and cream can echo cocoa-rich flavors; balance overall sweetness.
